title: Desire → anger → ruin; the peace at the end (2.62–2.72)
hook: eight links from a passing thought to losing yourself, and then an ocean that rivers pour into without changing

segments.voice: Yesterday, sthitaprajna: unshaken in sorrow, uncraving in joy, drawing in like a tortoise. Your line was unmoved. When did you draw in? Today, how steadiness gets lost, and where it ends. Day one hundred sixty-six.

Someone is scrolling, and there it is. A jacket, a car, somebody's vacation, somebody's job. A second's thought. Then another, later. By evening, wanting. By the weekend, not having it is quietly annoying. Then someone at dinner says the wrong thing, and the snap comes out of nowhere, and nobody's sure why. Long before phones, the Gita laid out that exact slide, link by link. It takes two verses. And then it shows the way out.
screen: `SCROLLING, AND THERE IT IS.` → `BY EVENING, WANTING IT.` → `A SNAP AT DINNER. WHY?`

segments.voice: Here's the chain, verses sixty-two and sixty-three. In Sanskrit it begins: dhyayato vishayan pumsah, sangas teshupajayate. When a person dwells on the objects of the senses, attachment to them is born. From attachment, desire, kama. From desire, anger, krodha, because desire that's blocked turns into anger. From anger, delusion. From delusion, memory wanders: you forget what you know, who you are. From the loss of memory, the power of discernment is destroyed. And when discernment is destroyed, the person is lost. Eight links, from dwelling on a thing to ruin. Notice where it starts. Not with doing anything wrong. With dwelling. The chain begins in attention. Which means it can be broken at the very first link. Then Krishna turns to the end of the chain, the peace. The one who moves among the things of the world with the senses under control, free of grasping and aversion, finds clarity, prasada, and in that clarity all sorrows end. For the unsteady there's no peace, and without peace, how can there be happiness? Then an image from the coast. The ocean is filled by rivers from every side, and yet it stays within its shores, unmoved. So the one into whom desires flow like rivers, and who stays unmoved, finds peace; not the one who chases desires. And the final verse: the one who lets go of desires, free of I and mine, attains peace. This is the Brahman state, Krishna says. Whoever reaches it, even at the very end, finds the stillness of Brahman. And that's chapter two, the chapter that holds everything.
screen: `IT BEGINS WITH DWELLING.` · `ATTACHMENT, DESIRE, ANGER, DELUSION.` · `MEMORY LOST, DISCERNMENT LOST, RUIN.` · `THE OCEAN, FILLED, STAYS IN ITS SHORES.` · then, large: `FREE OF I AND MINE: PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be the ocean. Settle, and breathe. Picture a wide, calm sea. Now let whatever wants to come, come: a want, an irritation, a plan, a craving. Each one is a river flowing in. Don't block it. Don't follow it upstream either. Just let it pour in, and notice that the sea stays the sea. Its level doesn't jump. Its shore doesn't move. If you catch yourself dwelling, sliding down the chain, just notice: ah, dwelling. And come back to the wide water. The bell holds the time.
Krodha. Anger, born from desire when it's blocked. The chain that starts with dwelling on a thing, and its end: the ocean, filled by rivers, unmoved, at peace.
Your line: the chain, and its end. Today, catch one craving at the first link, while you're still just dwelling, and let it flow in like a river to the sea. Day one hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Gita 2.62–2.63, the chain from dwelling on objects to ruin, is often taught in Hindu moral teaching, and the closing verses of chapter two, on the ocean and on peace, are recited in some homes as part of the sthitaprajna verses.

fork.setup: you've been thinking about something you want, on and off, all day. it's starting to irritate you that you don't have it. where does the Gita say to break the chain?
options: at the first link: the dwelling.
only after you get the thing.
fork.reveal: at the first link. the chain begins with dwelling on the object; everything after, desire, anger, delusion, grows from there.

original.note: Sanskrit: anger. in Gita 2.62, it's born from desire, kama.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't get angry.
what it means: anger is the middle of a chain that begins with dwelling on a thing, and ends in losing yourself. break it at the start.
what a scholar hears: smriti-bhramsha, the wandering of memory, then buddhi-nasha, the loss of discernment: the Gita's psychology of how people lose themselves.

notes: The chain (2.62–63): dhyana of objects → sanga → kama → krodha → sammoha → smriti-vibhrama → buddhi-nasha → pranasha. 'Eight links' counts from dwelling to ruin. Confirm.
2.70 ocean image; 2.71 nirmamo nirahankarah ('free of I and mine'); 2.72 brahmi sthiti and brahma-nirvana ('the stillness of Brahman'). Confirm glosses.
'Two thousand years before phones': the Gita's date is debated (often placed between roughly the 5th and 2nd centuries BCE). Confirm the phrasing is loose enough.
